claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi.
As-cast CoCrFeNiTi is an FCC solid solution.
Cast CoCrFeNiTi has high porosity and hardness of approximately 200 HV.
Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling produces sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement.
Milling-induced strain and refinement lower the energy barrier for an FCC-to-BCC transition.
VEC reduction and atomic-radius mismatch drive the proposed FCC-to-BCC transition.
CoCrFeNiTi has a VEC of approximately 7.4, near the FCC/BCC boundary, while its nominal VEC favors FCC.
Mechanical milling shifts the effective VEC and atomic-radius-mismatch parameters toward BCC stability.
High defect density and nanocrystallinity stabilize BCC CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed process uses 6 hours of milling followed by SPS at 1000°C for 10 minutes under 40 MPa.
SPS at 1000°C provides sufficient diffusion for rapid densification.
SPS at 1000°C maintains the milling-refined microstructure.
SPS at 1000°C prevents excessive precipitation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
Above 1050°C, grain growth accelerates and Ti-rich HCP phases precipitate, degrading mechanical properties.
Milling for less than 6 hours fails to induce the FCC-to-BCC transition.
The processed alloy will reach at least 98% of theoretical density.
The processed alloy will have a nanocrystalline BCC structure.
The processed alloy will attain Vickers hardness of at least 400 HV0.1.
Low-load Vickers testing can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
Hardness below 350 HV0.1 or an HCP fraction above 5 vol% decisively falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed 10 g indentation load corresponds to approximately HV0.01, but the outcome and falsification thresholds are expressed as HV0.1, which denotes a 100 g load.

The composition remains equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi, yet milling is claimed to reduce or shift VEC. Because nominal VEC is composition-derived, this conflicts unless a distinct, quantitatively defined electronic 'effective VEC' is intended.
The alloy is described as 'fully dense' while the specified acceptance threshold is only at least 98% of theoretical density.
